text: Lesson 19 described the hybrid loop conceptually. This lesson gets concrete about how that loop is actually implemented: treating a quantum circuit as one differentiable layer inside an otherwise ordinary PyTorch or TensorFlow model.

PennyLane's TorchLayer wraps a QNode so it behaves exactly like any other PyTorch module: it accepts a tensor, returns a tensor, and participates fully in PyTorch's autograd system. Calling backward on a loss that depends on this layer's output correctly computes gradients with respect to the circuit's parameters, using the parameter-shift rule under the hood, not classical backpropagation through actual circuit execution.

A typical small hybrid model looks like a sandwich. A classical linear layer reduces eight raw input features down to two numbers. Those two numbers get angle-encoded into a two-qubit variational circuit, the quantum layer, which outputs two expectation values. A final classical linear layer plus a sigmoid turns those two numbers into one class probability. Only the middle stage is quantum; the rest trains with ordinary backpropagation.

Three things reliably trip people up the first time. Data types: PennyLane circuits often expect float64, which doesn't match PyTorch's default float32, throwing a type error rather than a silently wrong answer. Batching: mixing an unsupported device with batched input can silently fall back to looping over the batch one sample at a time, which works but is much slower than it looks. And output shape: a two-qubit circuit measuring two observables returns a two-element output, not a scalar.

Next lesson asks the question that actually matters before you build one of these: Chapter 5 has shown you can splice a quantum circuit into a PyTorch model — that capability existing says nothing about whether doing so improves anything for a specific project.
